summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang; Tianzuo Li; Jiyeon Lee; Dahye Lim; Lianjie Xu; Yajie Liu; Jongcheol Seo; Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (design and synthesis of a novel protein topology)
summary.executive_summary: Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional topology can enhance stability. Artificial topological proteins have been made, but they usually contain multiple domains, which complicates the study of topological effects. The authors hypothesized that a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of chemical topology. They designed and synthesized a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically. The design rewired the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template. Synthesis was achieved in Escherichia coli cells using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to a linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability but with reduced activity (~5 U/mg versus ~14 U/mg), and exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science, demonstrating that the chemical topology of a protein domain can be changed without collapsing the fold and bringing profound changes in properties. The study provides a new scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and opens the possibility of converting linear proteins into single-domain catenanes with identical composition to the wild-type.

Most artificial topological proteins contain multiple domains. Multiple domains complicate the study of topological effects. A single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact. Single-domain topological proteins remain challenging to prepare. DHFR tolerates rethreading and retains similar structure and function.

Can a single-domain protein catenane be designed and synthesized? Can DHFR be converted into its single-domain catenane counterpart? Can chemical topology be changed without collapsing the fold? Will catenane topology preserve function and enhance stability? Will the original DHFR fold serve as the entangling template? Will catenanes retain catalytic capability despite entanglement? The model enzyme is DHFR from Escherichia coli. The target molecule is cat-DHFR with two rings. Cleavage occurs between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5. The cleavage site is at residues 88 and 89. The wild-type DHFR structure is PDB: 4KJJ. The Gaussian linking number matrix assesses entanglement. The split DHFR has a GLN of +0.726. The cat-DHFR has a GLN of +1.120. Genes are sub-cloned to pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. Cells are E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Expression is carried out at 16 o C for 20 h. Purification uses Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Further purification uses size exclusion chromatography. l-DHFR is the linear control with extra amino acids. Reconstitution efficiency depends on termini distance. The split-intein pairs may interfere with each other. The linker length affects reconstitution efficiency. The shortest linker yields ~12 mg/L of culture. Crystallization of cat-DHFR was attempted but failed. TEV protease cleavage converts cat-DHFR to fragments.

l-DHFR shows a single band at ~22 kDa. cat-DHFR shows a major band at less than 20 kDa. cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak in SEC. cat-DHFR has a more compact structure. cat-DHFR may have a dynamic structure. LC-MS confirms accurate molecular weights. cat-DHFR remains folded per far-UV CD. cat-DHFR has reduced CD intensities. cat-DHFR has positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. The single-side construct yields ~33% catenane. The site between residues 23 and 24 is most efficient. cat-DHFR has lower activity (~5 U/mg).

cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability. cat-DHFR has a Km ~5-fold that of l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a kcat ~38% that of l-DHFR. Catalytic efficiency is reduced by an order of magnitude. KD is ~173-fold larger for DHF. KD is ~14-fold larger for NADPH. KD for THF is ~3.6-fold larger. Linear proteins may become concatenated single-domain counterparts.

cat-DHFR has lower activity than l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has reduced CD intensities. cat-DHFR may have a dynamic structure. Crystallization of cat-DHFR failed. The cause of crystallization failure is uncertain. The single-side construct yields less catenane. The shortest linker reduces yield significantly. The method requires extensive optimization. The reduced activity may be restored by directed evolution. The binding affinity change is assumed.

A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be designed and synthesized in cells. cat-DHFR was designed and synthesized. The synthesis used split-inteins. The molecule contains few exogenous motifs. The topology was proven by protease cleavage. The crystallization failed. The activity is reduced. Linear proteins may become concatenated counterparts. The topology can be changed without collapsing the fold. The catenane topology enhances stability.
cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability but with reduced activity. cat-DHFR retains the catalytic capability. cat-DHFR has activity ~5 U/mg. l-DHFR has activity ~14 U/mg. The rethreaded DHFR shows no reducing activity. The split complex retains only 15% activity. The reduced activity is attributed to compromised affinity. The activity may be restored by directed evolution. The affinity is reduced for substrates and cofactors.
cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation. cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability. cat-DHFR preserves more activity in DMSO. l-DHFR preserves 74% activity in DMSO. cat-DHFR has reduced CD intensities. cat-DHFR may have a dynamic structure. Mechanical interlocking enhances thermal resilience. The conformational restriction enhances stability. The catenane topology reinforces folding.

Data And Code Availability
The sequence information is in the Supporting Information. The GLN matrices are in Figure S1. The kinetic parameters are in Table 1. The linker effects are in Figure S4. The single-side construct is in Figure S3a.

The method is generally robust before the linker becomes too short. The shortest linker reduces yield to ~12 mg/L. The single-side construct yields ~33% catenane. The site between residues 23 and 24 is most efficient. The circular permutation is necessary for correct reconstitution.

Figure 1a shows the cat-DHFR design. Figure 1b shows the gene cassette. Figure 2a shows the SDS-PAGE analysis. Figure 2b shows the SEC overlay. Figure 2c shows the LC-MS spectra. Figure 2d shows the far-UV CD spectra. Figure 2e shows the protease cleavage. Table 1 shows the binding affinity.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the design and synthesis of cat-DHFR. The strongest evidence is the retention of catalytic capability. The future path is directed evolution to restore activity.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara (Osaka Metropolitan University); Takashi Kobayashi (Chuo University); Tetsuji Dohi (Chuo University); Takeshi Yoshimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Norifumi Fujimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Daisuke Kiriya (Osaka Metropolitan University)
summary.field_subfield: 2D materials / optoelectronics (photoluminescence engineering of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides)
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials science / condensed matter physics)
summary.executive_summary: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) of the form MX 2 (M = Mo, W and X = S, Se) are attractive for thin, mechanically robust crystals with a three-atom layer thickness and a direct band gap at the K and Kʹ points, making them promising for optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. However, their poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity—caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline-lattice defects—limits their optical behavior. For sulfur-based compounds such as MoS 2 and WS 2 , PL enhancement has been largely established by chemical treatments including p-type dopants such as 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8-tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) and tetrafluoro-1,4-benzoquinone, and by superacid molecules such as bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI), which can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times. These methods decrease the probability of generating trions and enhance exciton-dominated emission, but they are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe 2 and WSe 2 , where only oleic acid and hydrohalic acid treatments or defect repairing have shown limited success. The authors of this study developed a universal postpreparation method that removes the substrate effect by coating monolayer TMDCs with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, which has a melting point of 42-45 °C. Because of the large thermal coefficient of paraffin, the stain is effectively applied to the TMDCs in the coating process, and the paraffin-coated monolayers show spontaneous fluctuation that, in an extreme case, forms the shape of a bundle. During this fluctuation and deformation, the substrate effect is removed, and PL intensity improves remarkably in both sulfur- and selenium-based compounds. For example, MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 show factors of enhancement of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold from the as-exfoliated flakes, respectively, and a monolayer WS 2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times through paraffin coating. The mechanism is attributed to a combination of strain induced by the volume change caused by the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin and the subsequent desorption of the monolayer flakes from the substrate, which is confirmed by Raman shifts of the Eʹ peak by about -0.72 cm -1 and the Aʹ peak by 1.03 cm -1 in 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 . This universal strategy extends the design of applying TMDCs as optoelectronic materials due to the transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility of the paraffin, and it is applicable to other 2D layered materials.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs are attractive for their thin, mechanically robust crystals with a direct band gap. Their poor PL intensity is a major drawback limiting optical applications. Sulfur-based compounds have established PL enhancement via chemical treatments. Selenium-based compounds lack effective PL enhancement strategies. No universal strategy exists for improving optical behavior across diverse 2D semiconductors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a universal method can enhance PL across sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The hypothesis is that paraffin coating removes the substrate effect and enhances PL universally. The predicted outcome is that spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect. The predicted mechanism involves strain from paraffin's high thermal expansion coefficient. The predicted result is large PL enhancement factors across all four compounds.

Methodological Details
The paraffin used has a melting point of 42-45 °C. The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C before coating. A spin coater was used to apply the paraffin coating. A heat blower was applied to keep the paraffin melted during spin coating. The prepared film is transparent, enabling optical observation and PL measurement. PL enhancement was observed on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates. Raman analysis was performed on 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 . The Eʹ peak represents in-plane vibrations sensitive to strain. The Aʹ peak represents out-of-plane vibrations sensitive to carrier concentration. The number of tested compounds and their enhancement factors are reported. The sample was surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides to prevent bundling. The sample was examined at room temperature over time.

Procedures And Architectures
The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C before being dropped onto the sample. A heat blower was used to keep the paraffin in a melted state during spin coating. The paraffin covers the entire monolayer, confirmed by optical microscopy. PL mapping confirmed enhancement across the whole plane with partial greater enhancement. A thick film of paraffin by simple casting resulted in a nontransparent glassy appearance. The paraffin coating was applied to all four monolayer TMDCs. The factor of enhancement was dependent on each sample. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively by about -0.72 cm -1 after paraffin coating. The Aʹ peak shifted positively by 1.03 cm -1 after paraffin coating. The PL intensity in the center was about 2.3 times greater than at the rim. The PL peak position around the center shifted 5-10 meV lower in energy than the rim. The deformation into a bundle occurs in an extreme case.

Key Results
MoS 2 showed a remarkable PL enhancement factor of 215 due to its low as-exfoliated signal. The PL enhancement factors were 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold for MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 . A monolayer WS 2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times through paraffin coating. The normalized PL spectrum showed a decrease in the trion-derived shoulder. The decrease in FWHM and upshift of the peak suggest decreased carrier concentration. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively by about -0.72 cm -1 indicating strain. The Aʹ peak shifted positively by 1.03 cm -1 indicating decreased carrier concentration. The PL intensity in the center was about 2.3 times greater than at the rim. The PL peak position around the center shifted 5-10 meV lower in energy than the rim. The folded bilayer area showed remarkable PL enhancement and a lower-energy PL peak. The Eʹ peak in the Raman spectra shifted to lower energy indicating strain. The PL enhancement is due to a combination of strain and desorption.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The PL enhancement is attributed to the removal of the substrate effect. The substrate effect is eliminated by deformation and desorption of the monolayer. The desorption is caused by the penetration of paraffin at the interface. The strain is induced by the volume change from the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin. The method is applicable to other 2D layered materials. The paraffin's transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility extend optoelectronic device design. The method is useful for straining thin 2D materials. The method is applicable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

Contradictions And Limitations
The enhancement factor is dependent on each sample, introducing variability. The PL enhancement is nonuniform across the monolayer plane. The enhancement depends on the state of the fluctuation. The deformation happens gradually and spontaneously, complicating reproducibility.

Claims
Paraffin coating provides a universal strategy for enhancing PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs. The method is applicable to all four compounds. The enhancement factors are large across all compounds. The method differs from past methods applicable only to sulfur-based TMDCs. The enhancement factor is dependent on each sample. The PL enhancement is nonuniform across the monolayer plane. The method extends the design of applying TMDCs as optoelectronic materials. The method is applicable to other 2D layered materials.
The PL enhancement is due to a combination of strain and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively indicating strain. The Aʹ peak shifted positively indicating decreased carrier concentration. The substrate effect is eliminated by deformation and desorption. The enhancement is nonuniform across the monolayer plane. The deformation happens gradually and spontaneously. The method is useful for straining thin 2D materials. The method is applicable for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The PL enhancement was observed on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates. A monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes was prevented from bending and bundling. The folded bilayer area showed remarkable PL enhancement.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the paraffin coating process on a spin coater. Figure 1b shows PL spectra for a monolayer WS 2 with about 36 times enhancement. Figures 1c and 1d show optical microscopy and PL mapping images. Figure 2a shows the band gaps and emission wavelengths of the as-exfoliated flakes. Figure 2b shows the factors of enhancement for each original monolayer flake. Figures 3a to 3d show optical microscope images of the deformation process. Figure 3e shows the PL spectra for the deformed sample. Figure 3f shows the removal of the substrate effect. Figure 4 shows the statistical information of Raman shifts. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides. Table 2 shows the Raman peak shifts.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a universal paraffin-coating method for enhancing PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs. 2. The strongest evidence is the large PL enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold for MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 . 3. summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.field_subfield: Astronomy: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study (single lunar occultation event)
summary.executive_summary: Harvey & Oldag (2007) present the first multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, obtained with the high-speed infrared spectrophotometer pMIRAS on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope during an immersion event on 28 Aug 2001. The authors found that the occultation fringes could not be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observations simultaneously probe the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. They used the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell, fitting both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yielded a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The density gradient was best described by ρ ∝ r−2 or the gradient derived by Ivezić & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The authors also derived a dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr, consistent with prior estimates. A notable tension emerged: the models could not fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. This work resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately, providing strong constraints on the inner dust shell structure. The findings support radiatively driven mass loss but reveal a discrepancy at far-infrared wavelengths that may reflect non-constant outflow. The study highlights the power of lunar occultations for high-angular-resolution diagnostics of circumstellar environments.

Executive Summary
Harvey & Oldag (2007) present the first multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, obtained with the high-speed infrared spectrophotometer pMIRAS on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope during an immersion event on 28 Aug 2001. The observations spanned a continuous wavelength range of 1–4µm with a time resolution of 8 msec, enabling milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors found that the occultation fringes could not be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observations simultaneously probe the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. They used the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell, fitting both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yielded a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The density gradient was best described by ρ ∝ r−2 or the gradient derived by Ivezić & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The authors also derived a dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr, consistent with prior estimates. A notable tension emerged: the models could not fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. This work resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately, providing strong constraints on the inner dust shell structure. The findings support radiatively driven mass loss but reveal a discrepancy at far-infrared wavelengths that may reflect non-constant outflow. The study highlights the power of lunar occultations for high-angular-resolution diagnostics of circumstellar environments.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars supplies heavy elements and solids to the ISM. AGB mass loss involves radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but details are poorly understood. Molecular line studies reveal periodic mass-loss variations producing 'rings' in radial distributions. Deep imaging has found similar phenomena in dust around IRC+10216. Studying inner circumstellar shells requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec. Most interferometric observations have used only one or two broad bands. Lunar occultations and multi-aperture interferometry reach milli-arcsecond resolutions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
What is the spatial structure of the circumstellar dust shell around AFGL 5440? Can a single-size model fit the occultation fringes, or is a shell required? What are the inner radius, temperature, and density gradient of the dust shell? What dust composition fits the SED, including the IRAS 60µm flux? Can the IRAS 60µm flux be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss? What dust mass-loss rate is implied by the optical depth and density gradient?

Methodological Details
The study observed the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440 (aka OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344). Observations were made during an immersion occultation event on 28 Aug 2001 at approximately 02:44:00 UT. The Moon elevation was 36°, the Sun 17° below the horizon, position angle 54°, and lunar phase 0.72. Observations used the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument is a long/wide slit, high-speed spectrophotometer using a NaCl prism. Light was imaged onto a 32×100 pixel portion of a 256² InSb array detector. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector was read-out every 8 msec with photon integration over essentially the full 8 msec. Observations covered 1–4µm with resolving power from ~20 at short wavelengths to ~100 at long wavelengths. On average, one pixel corresponds to λ/∆λ = 100. The plate scale in the spatial direction was 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm and background-limited longward of 3µm.

Procedures And Architectures
A typical observation consisted of taking 5000 frames centered on the occultation event. The buffer holds the most recent 5000 frames to accommodate errors in predicted event times. Predicted occultation times can be in error by up to 10 seconds due to lunar limb irregularities. The data reduction shifts images to the same wavelength/pixel scale via cross-correlation. Detector tilt relative to X/Y axes was removed during processing. Sky subtraction used sky measurements on either side of the stellar spectrum. The reduction produced a weighted average two pixels wide in the spectral direction. The end result was a sequence of ~100 light curves with a few hundred frames each. Wavelength calibration fit the NaCl dispersion function to J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima. The calibration accuracy was good to ±0.01λ throughout the 1–4µm region. No flux calibration was attempted due to variable efficiency and non-photometric conditions. Relative signal was compared to well-characterized stars, consistent with literature magnitudes within ±30%.

Key Results
A single-size uniform disk model could not fit the AFGL 5440 fringes across 1–4µm. An 11 mas uniform disk fit mid-range wavelengths (2.5–3.2µm) but failed at short and long wavelengths. The maximum dust temperature was constrained to Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models with Tmax below 900 K lacked hot dust to fit long-wavelength fringes. The radial density gradient was close to r−2 or the Ivezić & Elitzur radiatively driven wind gradient. The optical depth at 5µm was 0.5 ± 0.1 for the best-fitting model. The best dust composition included SiC with comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite. The dust mass-loss rate was 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr for DUSTY amorphous carbon optical constants. The inner dust shell radius was 3.7×10¹⁴ cm, or 11 mas at 2.25 kpc. The central star angular diameter was of order 3 mas at 2500 K ± 300 K. The dust emissivity was ε ∝ λ−1.3, consistent with amorphous carbon-rich dust. Groenewegen et al. derived a gas mass-loss rate of 3.1×10−5 M⊙/yr and dust mass-loss rate of 5.1×10−8 M⊙/yr.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observations resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately. The inner dust shell temperature near 950 K constrains the inner radius location. The inner radius is nearly a factor of two below expected dust condensation temperatures. The density gradient is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The dust mass-loss rate is consistent with prior estimates of 5–10×10−8 M⊙/yr. The inability to fit the IRAS 60µm flux without graphite is a strong constraint. The 60µm discrepancy may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate. This contrasts with Suh (1997), who proposed higher recent mass-loss rates.

Contradictions And Limitations
No flux calibration was attempted due to variable efficiency and non-photometric conditions. The ±30% uncertainty in stellar magnitudes limits absolute flux comparisons. The data were limited to accuracies on the order of ±2 mas. A discrepancy near 1.7µm for IRC+00233 remains unexplained. The IRAS 60µm flux could not be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss. The graphite requirement contradicts evidence against graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The dust composition range for amorphous carbon was not fully explored. The stellar photosphere details were not thoroughly examined. The IRAS LRS agreement was only superficial. The 60µm discrepancy explanation is beyond the scope of the study.

Claims
Lunar occultations with high-speed spectrophotometry can resolve the inner dust shell structure of carbon-rich AGB stars. The observations achieved milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The occultation fringes were fit by a circumstellar shell model. The inner dust shell radius was constrained to 11 mas. The IRAS 60µm flux could not be fit without graphite. The graphite requirement contradicts prior evidence. The method constrains the dust density gradient and mass-loss rate. The technique can be applied to other carbon-rich AGB stars.
The maximum dust temperature near 950 K is a strong constraint on the inner dust shell location. The best-fitting models had Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models below 900 K lacked hot dust to fit long-wavelength fringes. The inner radius is nearly a factor of two below condensation temperatures. Ivezić & Elitzur (1996) derived a lower inner dust shell temperature of ~750 K. The temperature constraint defines the inner edge of the dust shell. The result supports radiatively driven mass loss.
The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss, indicating a possible recent decrease in mass-loss rate. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The 60µm discrepancy may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate. The radial location of 60µm dust is 1 to a few arcseconds from the star. This contrasts with Suh (1997), who proposed higher recent mass-loss rates. The 60µm discrepancy may reflect non-constant outflow. The time scale is comparable to the IRC+10216 fluctuation period.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study explored more than 200 models to understand parameter effects. Models with r−1.8 came closer to the IRAS 60µm flux but fit the 5–20µm SED poorly. Models with r−2.2 fit the SED out to 20µm but had worse IRAS 60µm fits. The outer radius makes no difference at λ < 60µm if at least 100 times the inner radius. Both MRN and KMH grain size distributions produced reasonable fits. A model without graphite fit the SED but gave a poor occultation fit.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for a 4.5 mas uniform disk model. Figure 2 shows χ² and signal-to-noise ratio as a function of wavelength. Figures 3 and 4 show HD 155292 uniform-disk fits with sizes less than 3 mas. Figure 5 shows AFGL 5440 light curves indicating a single size is unlikely to fit. Figures 7 and 8 show the best-fitting model fits to the SED and occultation light curves. Figure 9 shows the quality of the fit versus wavelength. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fitting model. Figures 11 and 12 show the best-fitting model without graphite. Figures 13 and 14 show a model that fits the SED but poorly fits the occultation.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: First multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of AFGL 5440 resolved the inner dust shell structure. 2. The strongest evidence: The maximum dust temperature of 950 K ± 50 K and density gradient of r−2 strongly constrain the inner dust shell. 3. The future path: The IRAS 60µm discrepancy may require graphite or non-constant outflow, pointing to further study of mass-loss variations.

summary.title: Green-Schwarz, Nambu-Goto Actions, and Cayley's Hyperdeterminant
summary.authors: Hitoshi Nishino and Subhash Rajpoot
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes that the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model action for the N = 2 superstring, whose target space-time is D = 2+2, can be re-expressed in a Nambu-Goto (NG)-type form whose kinetic term is exactly the square root of Cayley's hyperdeterminant. The authors build on a recent result showing that the NG action in D = 2+2 possesses a manifest global SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) symmetry, realized through the hyperdeterminant of the superspace pull-back. They argue that the GS formulation is preferable to the Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond (NSR) one because the latter is obstructed by fermionic superpartners on the world-sheet, whereas the GS formulation lacks explicit world-sheet supersymmetry and can be shown to be classically equivalent to the NSR one on the light-cone via fermionic kappa-symmetry. The central technical achievement is the elimination of the zweibein (2D metric) from the GS action using its non-algebraic field equation, in a manner analogous to deriving the NG action from the Polyakov action. After this elimination, the remaining NG-term is identified as the square root of the hyperdeterminant Det(Πiα.α), which is manifestly invariant under the [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The authors also demonstrate that the target superspace D = (2, 2; 2, 2) accommodates the self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills (SDSYM) multiplet with N = (1, 1) space-time supersymmetry, which is relevant to the conjecture that all bosonic integrable models in D ≤ 3 are generated by self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Importantly, the paper explicitly refrains from claiming quantum-level equivalence, noting that even the NG-to-Polyakov equivalence is not well established at the quantum level. Instead, it asserts only classical-level symmetries: the fermionic kappa-symmetry and the manifest [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The derivation is carried out entirely in terms of the fundamental superfield ZM and the superspace pull-back ΠiA, with no involvement of the 2D metric gij, the zweibein ei(j), or the factor Ω. A notable by-product is the confirmation that the Virasoro conditions follow as first-order constraints at the classical level, consistent with prior results in the NG formulation. The paper also points out that the hidden discrete triality symmetry present in the NG action is absent in the N = 2 string due to the WZNW-term. The work emphasizes that the signature D = 2+2 is crucial because SO(2, 2) is isomorphic to SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR), unlike SO(3, 1) which is isomorphic to SL(2, C). The authors acknowledge W. Siegel and the referee for noticing mistakes in an earlier version, underscoring the exploratory nature of the work. Overall, the paper contributes a manifestly symmetric classical reformulation of the N = 2 GS superstring, linking it to Cayley's hyperdeterminant and to the broader framework of self-dual Yang-Mills theory and supersymmetric integrable models, while carefully delineating the limits of its claims regarding quantum equivalence.

Research Context
Cayley's hyperdeterminant has found applications in physics beyond its mathematical origins. The hyperdeterminant has been used in quantum information theory and black hole entropy. The NG action in D = 2+2 was recently shown to possess a manifest [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The hyperdeterminant realizes this symmetry via the square root of the determinant of an inner product of pull-backs. The D = 2+2 dimensions are the consistent target space-time of the N = 2 NSR superstring. The NSR formulation is obstructed for rewriting purely in terms of a determinant due to fermionic superpartners. The GS formulation is classically equivalent to the NSR formulation on the light-cone via kappa-symmetry. The D = (2, 2; 2, 2) superspace accommodates the self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills multiplet. The conjecture links self-dual Yang-Mills theory to all bosonic integrable models in D ≤ 3.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper asks whether the N = 2 GS sigma-model action can be re-expressed in an NG-type form with a hyperdeterminant kinetic term. The hypothesis is that eliminating the zweibein yields the NG action as the square root of the hyperdeterminant. The authors hypothesize that this reformulation is manifestly invariant under the [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The authors hypothesize that the GS formulation is advantageous over the NSR one for this rewriting. The authors hypothesize that the fermionic kappa-symmetry criterion is satisfied for light-cone equivalence. The authors predict that the [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry is inherent in the N = 2 GS action when the zweibein is eliminated. The authors predict that the target superspace supports N = (1, 1) space-time supersymmetry. The authors predict that the Virasoro conditions follow as first-order constraints at the classical level. The authors predict that the hidden triality symmetry is absent due to the WZNW-term. The authors predict that the signature D = 2+2 is crucial for the SL(2, IR) structure.

Methodological Details
The target space-time is D = 2+2, and the target superspace is D = (2, 2; 2, 2). The superspace has 2+2 bosonic coordinates plus 2 chiral and 2 anti-chiral fermionic coordinates. The N = 2 refers to world-sheet supersymmetries in the NSR formulation, not space-time supersymmetry. The fundamental field variable is the superfield ZM, with no involvement of the 2D metric or zweibein. The world-sheet coordinates are i, j, ··· = 0, 1, and the light-cone indices are +, −. The local Lorentz coordinates are (i), (j), ··· = (0), (1), with metric η(i)(j) = diag. (+, −). The bosonic local Lorentz indices are a, b, ··· = 0, 1, 2, 3. The fermionic indices are α, β, ··· = 1, 2 for chiral and .α, .β, ··· = .1, .2 for anti-chiral. The curved fermionic indices are µ, ν, ··· = 1, 2, 3, 4. The superspace pull-back is defined as ΠiA ≡(∂iZM)EM A.

The transformation behavior of these functions under Γ0(p) is controlled via a character ψ, and the ramification at cusps is analyzed through Fourier expansions. The note also treats the special cases p = 2, 3 and the case p ≡ 11 mod 12, which requires a different construction using triplets of eta functions. The theoretical implication is that allowing cusp ramification doubles the maximal unramified abelian degree, and the method illustrates how generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) can be used to build explicit modular functions with prescribed ramification. The paper is purely theoretical, with no numerical experiments, datasets, or code, and no bibliography is provided, so top_influential_citations is empty.

Research Context
The setting is the theory of maximal unramified abelian coverings of curves over number fields. For a smooth geometrically integral curve Y admitting a degree one divisor, the maximal unramified abelian extension k(Y)ur,ab of its function field is well defined. The geometric part π1(Y )ab,geo of the abelian fundamental group is finite, a key structural fact. Mazur's theorem establishes the Shimura covering as the maximal unramified abelian covering of X0(p). The gap is that allowing ramification at cusps may permit a strictly larger covering than the Shimura one.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the cuspidal locus Y0(p) can exceed the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p). The hypothesis is that such a covering exists and is cyclic of degree 2Np, factoring through the Shimura covering by a degree-two cover. The predicted outcome is that this covering is geometrically maximal over Y0(p) and ramified only at cusps. The degree doubling is predicted to arise from a Z/2Z extension of the Shimura covering. The construction is predicted to rely on generalized Dedekind eta functions generating a quadratic extension.

Methodological Details
The objects of study are the modular curves X0(p) and X1(p) as smooth proper geometrically integral curves over Q. The base curve Y0(p) is the open subscheme of X0(p) obtained by removing the two cusps 0 and ∞. The Shimura covering f_p : X2(p) → X0(p) has degree Np := (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12). The target covering f'p : X'2(p) → X0(p) has degree 2Np, twice the Shimura degree. The construction assumes p is an odd prime with p ≥ 5, with p = 2, 3 handled separately. The generalized Jacobian eJ := Jac(X, D) with modulus D is a semi-abelian variety fitting in an exact sequence. The torsion module MTor := Hom(TeJ, Q/Z(1)) is a divisible torsion Gk-module. The character group LD := Hom(GD, Gm,k) is free abelian of rank rD := Σ(x∈D)[k(x):k] − 1. The abelian fundamental group satisfies π1(Y )ab,geo ≅ Hom(MµTor(−1), Q/Z). The key group Σ(f) := ker(f*: J(k) → J'(k)) controls the maximal unramified abelian subcovering. The maximal unramified abelian covering has Galois group Hom(Σ(f), Q/Z(1)). The generalized Dedekind eta function Eg is defined via an infinite product with the second Bernoulli polynomial.

Procedures And Architectures
The proof of Theorem 1.2.2 is organized into a first reduction, eta-function preparation, and the modular curve X'2(p). The first reduction shows that a degree-2Np cyclic cover satisfying condition (2) automatically satisfies condition (1). The generalized Dedekind eta function Eg satisfies Eg+N = E−g = −Eg. The eta functions transform under Γ0(N) with a root-of-unity factor ε(a,bN,c,d) and an exponential term. Products of eta functions with Σg eg ≡ 0 mod 12, Σg geg ≡ 0 mod 2, Σg g²eg ≡ 0 mod 2N are modular functions on Γ1(N). The function F_h(τ) is defined as a product of 6/ℓ powers of ℓ eta functions E_{g^j k h}. The functions F_h satisfy F_h = F_{−h} = F_{p+h}. The transformation law F_h(γτ) = ψ(γ)F_{ah}(τ) holds for γ ∈ Γ0(p). The character ψ is defined by ψ(γ) = (−1)^{a+d−1} if c is odd, (−1)^b if c is even. The group Γ'2(p) is normal in Γ0(p) with quotient cyclic of order 2k. The order of F^2_h at any cusp of X2(p) is odd and zero elsewhere. For p ≡ 11 mod 12, a triplet construction Gh = (E_{h1}E_{h2}E_{h3})² with h1²+h2²+h3² ≡ 0 mod p is used.

Key Results
The main theorem constructs a cyclic covering of degree 2Np that is geometrically maximal over Y0(p). The covering f'p factors as f'p = f_p ∘ π_p with π_p a degree-two cover unramified outside cusps. The order of MµTor(−1) is either Np or 2Np, establishing the doubling possibility. The covering X'2(p) → X2(p) ramifies precisely at each cusp. The function field Q(X'2(p)) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of F^2_h. The order of F^2_h at a non-cusp point is zero, so F^2_h is unramified away from cusps. The order of F^2_h at a cusp of width p is 1, contributing to odd ramification. The order of F^2_h at a cusp of width 1 is congruent to p ≡ 1 mod 2, confirming odd order. The group Γ'2(p) gives Γ0(p)/Γ'2(p) cyclic of order 2k, matching the degree 2Np. For p ≡ 11 mod 12, the triplet construction yields G^2_h a modular function on X1(p) with odd cusp order. The function z(τ) = (η(τ)/η(pτ))^{12/(p−1,12)} is a modular function on Γ'2(p) but not on Γ2(p). The relation between F_h and z is z(τ) = ±∏_{j=0}^{k−1} F_{g^j}.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result shows that allowing cusp ramification doubles the maximal unramified abelian degree from Np to 2Np. The doubling arises because (LD ⊗ Q/Z)µ(−1) ≅ Z/2Z contributes an extra Z/2Z factor. The geometric maximality over Y0(p) follows from the isomorphism π1(Y )ab,geo ≅ Hom(MµTor(−1), Q/Z). The construction demonstrates that generalized Dedekind eta functions can build explicit modular functions with prescribed cusp ramification. The factorization through the Shimura covering shows the new covering extends Mazur's maximal unramified cover. The degree-two extension π_p is unramified outside cusps, isolating the cusp contribution to the doubling.

Contradictions And Limitations
The construction is restricted to odd primes p ≥ 5, with p = 2, 3 handled by a separate elementary argument. The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 requires a different construction, indicating methodological sensitivity to p mod 12. The exact value of the extra Z/2Z factor is not fully pinned down, leaving Np vs 2Np as a dichotomy.

Claims
A geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) over Q exists and is cyclic of degree 2Np, extending the Shimura covering. The main theorem asserts existence of a cyclic covering of degree 2Np. The covering is geometrically maximal over Y0(p). The covering factors through the Shimura covering. The order of MµTor(−1) could be Np rather than 2Np, so doubling is conditional. The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 requires a different construction, limiting uniformity. The maximal unramified abelian degree over Y0(p) is exactly twice that over X0(p). Generalized Dedekind eta functions provide explicit generators for the quadratic extension. The method extends to other modular curves with cuspidal ramification allowed.
The function field Q(X'2(p)) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of an explicit rational function. The extension is quadratic over Q(X2(p)). The generator is a square root of F^2_h. F^2_h is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q. The function z(τ) provides an alternative generator, showing non-uniqueness of the generator. The quadratic structure explains the degree-two extension π_p. Explicit generators enable concrete computation of the covering.

The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 is handled by a separate construction, showing methodological robustness across residue classes. The case p = 2, 3 is handled by an elementary map Gm → Gm, x ↦ x². The proof first assumes p ∤ 11 mod 12, then extends to the remaining case.

summary.executive_summary: Rare variants are hypothesized to contribute substantially to the heritability of complex diseases, yet rare variant association studies (RVAS) frequently lack statistical power, particularly in small-to-medium cohorts or when variants explain only a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing enable genome-wide investigation of rare variants, but existing association tests struggle when effect sizes are small or heterogeneous. This paper introduces BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test based on Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), implemented within the rvGWAS framework. Unlike prior methods, BATI flexibly incorporates individual or variant-specific features as covariates while performing efficient full-model inference. The authors argue that integrating meaningful biological context, such as functional annotation, substantially improves power. They developed a semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing simulator combining thousands of real datasets with ClinVar-derived disease variants to create realistic case-control cohorts for benchmarking. Using breast cancer risk cohorts (1000GP and Iberian), they benchmarked BATI against Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O, MiST, HBMR, and demonstrated that BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, including when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. They propose using the difference in Deviance Information Criterion (ΔDIC) for model selection, with a threshold of ΔDIC > 10 recommended. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, they identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The authors contend that combining real WES background noise with real disease variants yields more realistic benchmarks than purely simulated data. This work provides a comprehensive, user-friendly framework for RVAS analysis, integrating quality control, filtering, stratification detection, functional annotation, and multiple association tests. The central claim is that leveraging variant characteristics through fast, accurate INLA estimation enables BATI to outperform existing methods on realistic cohorts. The study highlights that differences between methods are most pronounced at low variance-explained levels, where some methods show near-zero power. Overall, the paper advances both methodology and practical application, offering a flexible testing approach that can be extended in future work.

Research Context
Rare variants are thought to play an important role in the etiology of complex diseases. RVs may explain a significant fraction of the missing heritability in genetic disease studies. RVs are more likely to affect protein structure, stability, or function than common variants. RVAS facilitate identification of disease loci based on burden of rare and damaging variants. RVAS still lack power when cohorts are small to medium-sized and if genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA can flexibly integrate variant characteristics while maintaining computational efficiency. BATI allows integration of individual or variant-specific features as covariates, while efficiently performing inference based on full model estimation. The hypothesis is that BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic cohorts, especially when using meaningful biological context such as functional annotation. BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios in which competing tests fail to identify risk genes. BATI is particularly powerful when risk variants in sum explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The authors predict that leveraging variant characteristics and fast INLA estimation will outperform existing methods on realistic WES cohorts.

Methodological Details
The study presents BATI, a Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. BATI was implemented using the R-INLA project, with R package INLA version 17.06.20. The method is implemented as part of the Rare Variant Genome Wide Association Study (rvGWAS) framework. rvGWAS combines quality control, interactive filtering, detection of data stratification, integration of functional variant annotations, and four commonly used rare variant association tests. The framework includes Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC and MiST, as well as the two Bayesian alternatives, HBMR and BATI. The framework supports rare variant association for genes or any other biological unit such as promoters. A new disease cohort simulator was developed by combining thousands of real WES datasets from various studies with known risk variants. The simulator randomly assigns WES samples to the case or control group and introduces predisposition variants found in ClinVar. Two large datasets were used as basis for the simulation: 1000GP and the Iberian cohort. For 1000GP, half of the samples were selected as cases and the other half as controls. For the Iberian cohort, one third was selected as cases and two thirds as controls. ClinVar was queried for breast cancer risk variants annotated as exonic or splicing.

Procedures And Architectures
Variants with MAF higher than 0.01 in any ancestry population were removed using EVS, 1000GP or ExAC databases. RVAS tests were performed on randomly split cohorts without introduced ClinVar risk variants to obtain comparable significance thresholds. Significance thresholds were calculated for Burden, KBAC, SKAT-O and MiST translating to 5%, 0.1% and 0.01% TIER. For HBMR and BATI, thresholds were calculated for Bayes factor resulting in the same ΔDIC TIER levels. Thresholds were estimated across 10 random cohort splits, using the test-specific median as thresholds. Model selection uses the difference in Deviance Information Criterion (ΔDIC) between the null and alternative models. A ΔDIC threshold of greater than 10 is recommended to reject the null hypothesis. S datasets were generated by randomly shuffling cases and controls, with S = 10 used for model selection. The benchmark study used 100 simulations of risk variants for each gene separately. The 1000GP cohort results are presented in Fig 3 and Table 2, while the Iberian cohort is in Supplementary S9 Fig.

Most tests perform slightly worse due to the smaller size of the Iberian cohort (1,167 vs 1,810 total individuals). BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size. At a low VE of 0.5% and a strict TIER of 0.01%, all methods except BATI show power close to 0. BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes, with a median power of 55%. All methods except MiST identify all risk genes at 0.01% TIER in the 2% VE setting. BATI calls most genes with TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%, and all genes at TIER 0.1% with greater than 80% power. Burden, KBAC and SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2, while HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2 and PALB2 already at TIER 0.1%. Differences between methods when VE is low (1% and 0.5%) are substantially more profound than previously appreciated. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER thresholds. Burden, KBAC and SKAT-O fail to predict the same genes at 0.5% VE, namely BRCA2, BARD1 and CHEK2. BATI outperforms existing RVAS test methods on realistic WES cohorts using real disease variants in 8 breast cancer risk genes. BATI strongly benefits from the inclusion of variant characteristics as covariates. BATI's gain in power is significant when risk genes contain mostly loss-of-function variants. BATI still performs at least as good as other methods when testing genes containing mostly missense variants. Leveraging variant characteristics and fast, accurate INLA estimation enables BATI to outperform existing methods. BATI represents a flexible testing approach that can be further extended and enhanced in the future. Combining real WES background noise with real disease variants yields more realistic benchmarks than purely simulated data. The use of random causal variants hampers benchmarking of methods that leverage characteristics of causal disease variants. It is likely beneficial to combine Burden- and SKAT-type methods with completely different approaches to compensate for weaknesses.

The benchmark relies on semi-synthetic data, which may not fully capture real-world complexity. The study focuses on breast cancer risk genes, limiting generalizability to other diseases. summary.title: Search for High-Energy Gamma-Ray Emission from Anomalous X-ray Pulsar, 4U 0142+61
summary.authors: Sinem Şaşmaz Müş and Ersin Göğüş
summary.executive_summary: Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated neutron stars powered by ultra-strong magnetic fields, and until 2004 they were known only as soft X-ray emitters. The discovery of a hard X-ray/soft gamma-ray component from several AXPs (1E 1841-045, 4U 0142+61, 1RXS J170849.0-400910) provided important insight but posed a serious challenge to explain its origin. The physical mechanism of the hard emission component has still not been fully resolved, motivating this work. This paper investigates the high-energy gamma-ray properties of the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, using data collected with the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on board Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to establish the spectral behavior of the source on a very broad energy span and search for pulsed emission. The LAT operates in the energy band of 20 MeV-300 GeV and has been operating as an all sky monitor since 2008 August 4. The authors accumulated LAT data within a 15° radius centered at 4U 0142+61, collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure time of ~31.7 Ms, and performed unbinned likelihood analysis using ScienceTools v9r15p2 with P6 V3 DIFFUSE as the instrumental response. They also employed contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations to obtain the spin ephemeris of the source, selecting 53 RXTE observations performed between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30 with a total exposure time of about 196 ks. The search for persistent emission yielded no significant detection: the Test Statistics (TS) value is ~0.23 for the 15° region (detection significance less than 1σ) and ~3 for the 2° region (detection significance less than 4σ). The 3σ flux upper limits with a power law index 2.5 are 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band and 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band. For pulsed emission, both LAT pulse profiles are consistent with random fluctuations with respect to its mean, and the 3σ upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% in the 0.2-1.0 GeV band and 2.3% in the 1.0-10.0 GeV band. The lower energy LAT passband (30-200 MeV) also resulted with no evidence of pulsed emission; the 3σ RMS pulsed fraction upper limit is 1.6%. The authors constructed the νFν spectrum of the source in the 15 keV-10 GeV range by adopting the hard X-ray spectrum presented in den Hartog et al. (2008) and placing the upper limits calculated in this work. The upper limit curve is a power law with an index of -0.76, and these two curves intersect with each other at ~1.1 MeV, which is an upper limit to the spectral break energy. This estimate is in accordance with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007) and the quantum electrodynamics model by Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b). The main conclusion is that no significant high-energy gamma-ray emission is detected, but the obtained upper limits help constrain existing physical models. The results are important because our LAT upper limits are much lower than high pulsed fraction (up to 100%) seen in hard X-rays with INTEGRAL (den Hartog et al. 2008).

Research Context
AXPs are intriguing sources since their discovery in early 80s. Until 2004, AXPs were known as strong emitters of soft X-rays only. The discovery of hard X-ray component from AXPs posed a serious challenge to explain its origin. The physical mechanism of the hard emission component has still not been fully resolved. AXPs are commonly regarded as young isolated neutron stars powered by extremely strong magnetic fields. Strong magnetic fields can efficiently slow these young systems down via magnetic breaking. Establishing spectral shapes on a wide energy range is crucial to understand the hard emission component. The LAT enables investigation of high-energy behavior of these sources with unprecedented data quality.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal is to investigate the high-energy gamma-ray properties of the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61. The study aims to establish the spectral behavior of the source on a very broad energy span. The study aims to search for pulsed emission from 4U 0142+61. The study presents results of detailed search for the persistent and pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission from 4U 0142+61. The predicted outcome is no significant detection, but upper limits to the persistent high-energy gamma-ray emission flux. The upper limits help constrain existing physical models of the hard emission component. The hard X-ray emission could originate from a plasma corona around the magnetar (Beloborodov & Thompson 2007). The fast-mode breakdown model (Heyl & Hernquist 2005a,b) predicts a break energy around 1 MeV. The upscattered surface thermal X-ray photons model (Baring & Harding 2007) is another attempt to explain the hard emission.

Methodological Details
The study uses LAT data on board Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The LAT operates in the energy band of 20 MeV-300 GeV. The LAT is a pair conversion telescope with a high-resolution silicon tracker, calorimeter, anticoincidence detector, programmable trigger and data acquisition system. The LAT has been operating as an all sky monitor in high-energy gamma-rays since 2008 August 4. The LAT covers the full sky in approximately every 3 hours. The LAT data were accumulated within a 15° radius centered at 4U 0142+61. The data were collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29. The exposure time is ~31.7 Ms. A 2° radius region around the source was used for spectral analysis to avoid contamination from nearby bright sources. The unbinned likelihood analysis used ScienceTools v9r15p2 with P6 V3 DIFFUSE as the instrumental response. The maximum zenith angle was set to 105° to eliminate background gamma-rays due to the Earth limb. The galactic diffuse emission was modeled with gll iem v02.fit.

The diffuse gamma-ray emission from the Milky Way was modeled with the latest model. The isotropic iem v02.txt was used to account for the extragalactic isotropic diffuse emission and residual instrumental background. The spectral fits and flux calculations were done with the python version of gtlike, pyLikelihood. Photon arrival times were converted to that at the solar system barycenter using gtbary of ScienceTools. The precise spin ephemeris was obtained using contemporaneous RXTE observations. Only the PCA observations were employed, sensitive to photon energies between 2-60 keV. 53 RXTE observations were selected performed between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30. The RXTE observations were performed under Program IDs P93019, P94019 and P05019. The total exposure time of all selected observations is about 196 ks. Events were extracted in the 2-10 keV range collected with the PCA. The arrival times were converted to the solar system barycenter using faxbary tool of HEASoft 6.8. A Fourier based epoch folding technique was used to obtain the spin ephemeris.

The spectral break upper limit is consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007). summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Molecular diagnostics / metagenomics (SARS-CoV-2 detection and sequencing)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the limitations of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) as the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, which reportedly identifies only 47-59% of true positive cases due to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or primer-binding mutations. The authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based method using 343 primer pairs to improve sensitivity and accommodate diverse clinical settings. The assay produces clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, enabling direct identification of positives by electrophoresis. The method amplified the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens, and detected mutations through next-generation sequencing. Additionally, a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method was developed in parallel, requiring modest sequencing depth for uncovering SARS-CoV-2 mutational diversity and potentially novel or emerging isolates. The authors built mathematical models to estimate limits of detection (LOD), finding that RT-PCR could only detect 4.8 copies at 95% probability, while their multiplex-PCR panel could theoretically detect 0.29 copies using both overlapping primer pools. Experimentally, the method detected 1.1 copies with 56% probability, exceeding the predicted 12% based on a 6% amplification efficiency assumption. The study demonstrated that full-genome sequencing could be achieved with as few as 50,000 total reads per library, covering at least 58% of the genome at 100X. Mutations were detected from samples with viral loads ranging from 8 to half a million copies, and the D614G mutation was found in 11 of 13 specimens. The metagenomic method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA while requiring only ~0.6M total reads per library, without additional host depletion. The study highlights the superior sensitivity and specificity of the multiplex-PCR approach compared to RT-PCR, and its potential for detecting novel pathogens. However, the study has limitations, including the lack of UMI usage, which may introduce noise from PCR amplification, and the caution needed in interpreting intra-host mutations obtained with low viral copy inputs and low sequencing depth. The findings have significant implications for improving SARS-CoV-2 diagnostics and surveillance, particularly in resource-limited settings where high sequencing depth may be economically prohibitive.

The findings have significant implications for improving SARS-CoV-2 diagnostics and surveillance, particularly in resource-limited settings where high sequencing depth may be economically prohibitive.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis due to its ease of use and high sensitivity. RT-PCR reportedly identifies only 47-59% of true positive cases, indicating significant diagnostic limitations. Low detection rates may result from low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or primer-binding mutations. Full-length genome sequencing is essential for surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 evolution and containment of community spread. Genome sequence analysis has guided policy-making and management procedures for SARS-CoV-2. Multiplex PCR has been shown to be an efficient and low-cost method with high coverage, specificity, and sensitivity. Metagenomic approaches require very high sequencing depth, making them economically prohibitive as diagnostic assays.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a multiplex-PCR-based method can improve sensitivity over RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection. The hypothesis is that multiplex PCR, by simultaneously targeting hundreds of regions, has significantly higher sensitivity than RT-PCR. The method may detect nucleotide fragments resulting from degraded viral genomes and tolerate genomic variations. The authors hypothesized that their SARS-CoV-2 panel could detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability using 172 primer pairs. Using both overlapping primer pools would lead to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The authors hypothesized that the actual amplification efficiency of multiplex PCR would be higher than the estimated 6%. The metagenomic method could detect SARS-CoV-2 with moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted by researchers from Paragon Genomics Inc, Stanford University, and Children's Hospital Los Angeles. The SARS-CoV-2 genome size used for modeling was 29,903bp (NC_045512.2). The primary detection method comprised 343 pairs of specific primers. The first primer pool consisted of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers with an average amplicon length of 99bp. The amplicons spanned the entire genome with an average 76±10bp gap between adjacent amplicons. A second pool of 171 primer pairs overlapped with the gaps of the first pool for full genome coverage. The study used 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens previously diagnosed positive by RT-PCR. Viral load ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL across the specimens. The copy number of plasmids was determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) with a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. Two plasmids containing the full sequence of the S and N genes were used to validate the multiplex PCR method. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms, reporting only those detected by both methods.

Procedures And Architectures
The mathematical model assumed 99% RT-PCR efficiency to estimate the limit of detection. The model predicted RT-PCR could only detect 4.8 copies at 95% probability. The model assumed 6% amplification efficiency for single-strand cDNA in multiplex PCR. The workflow involved secondary PCR amplification during which sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers were added. PCR products were analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize potential positives with defined peak sizes. The two plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy. The library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. Random hexamer-adapters were used to amplify DNA or cDNA targets in the metagenomic method. Paragon Genomics' background removal reagent was used to remove non-specific amplification products. Paragon Genomics' reverse transcription reagents converted RNA into cDNA to reduce human ribosomal RNA. The library was sequenced at 0.6 million reads per sample in the metagenomic method. No UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification.

Key Results
The multiplex PCR method detected library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids, demonstrating a wide dynamic range. Quantification demonstrated a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids. The library yield started to saturate when the copy number reached 1,700. In contrast, RT-PCR detected quantities of a single target on the S gene rapidly dropped when using 2.85 copies. The experimentally observed probability to detect 1.1 copies was 56%, significantly higher than the predicted 12%. Recovered reads were within a range of about 20-fold relative depth with about 1.4 to 2.8 plasmids. Approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids, 77% with 2.8 copies, and 37% with 0.6 copies. About 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. 98-99% of genomes were covered at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies at an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. At least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X with 150,000 total reads. 86% of the genome was covered at 100X with 100,000 total reads. Even at 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The higher experimental detection probability suggests the actual amplification efficiency of multiplex PCR exceeds the estimated 6%. The method tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2, unlike RT-PCR which may fail due to primer-binding mutations. The superior uniformity of amplicon amplification and recovery manifested the high coverage of the multiplex PCR method. The metagenomic method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes while requiring only ~0.6M total reads per library. The 10-fold difference in coverage has been routinely observed with the multiplex PCR technology. Increasing sequencing depth alone might not improve the coverage of the targeted regions further. The high specificity argues strongly that the panel could be expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA.

Contradictions And Limitations
No UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification, which may introduce noise from PCR amplification. Intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification, even with a 20% cutoff. The occurrence of noise may be exacerbated by low viral copy inputs in the multiplex PCR. Group 2 had low copy numbers and low read depth per amplicon, with considerably higher apparent intra-host mutations. Recurring mutations in group 2 might not be true intra-host mutations, possibly caused by low copy number inputs. Copy number and sequencing depth should be cautiously considered when a mutation is found to have low %AF. Some true intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% might be missed due to the 20% cutoff. The coverage of one genome from a sample with 5,000 estimated viral copies was lower than expected. The low coverage might have been caused by poor sample quality from processing or handling the viral RNA. It is still necessary to verify and validate the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses by the metagenomic method.

Claims
The multiplex-PCR-based method is more sensitive than RT-PCR and can detect SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers. The method detected library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. The experimental detection probability of 56% exceeded the predicted 12% based on 6% efficiency. The method tolerated mutations in SARS-CoV-2, unlike RT-PCR. The theoretical calculation gave only a 12% chance to detect 1.1 copies based on 6% efficiency. The amplification efficiency could be lower if the template is one single strand of cDNA. The panel could be expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses.

summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a survey-style account of image noise and the algorithms used to remove it, culminating in a comparative performance evaluation of several denoising filters. summary.title: The Cauchy problem for a class of two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equations governing anti-plane shear motions in elastic materials
summary.authors: H. A. Erbay, S. Erbay, and A. Erkip
summary.executive_summary: This paper analyzes the Cauchy (initial value) problem for a general class of two-dimensional nonlinear nonlocal wave equations that model anti-plane shear motions in nonlocal elasticity. The nonlocal character is encoded through a convolution integral in the spatial variables, whose Fourier transform is nonnegative and satisfies a growth condition at infinity. The authors establish well-posedness, conditions for global existence, and conditions for finite-time blow-up of solutions for initial data in L2 Sobolev spaces. The central object is the equation w_tt = (β * ∂F/∂w_x)_x + (β * ∂F/∂w_y)_y, where F is a nonlinear function of |∇w|² = w_x² + w_y² with F(0) = 0, and β is an integrable kernel whose Fourier transform b_β(ξ) satisfies 0 ≤ b_β(ξ) ≤ C(1 + |ξ|²)^(-r/2) with r ≥ 2. The parameter r governs the smoothness of β and, as r increases, the regularizing effect of the nonlocal behavior increases. Local existence and uniqueness are proven by converting the problem into a system of Banach space-valued ordinary differential equations and using the operator K defined by the convolution and nonlinear terms. Global existence is established via conservation of energy, requiring a positivity condition F(u) ≥ -ku together with sufficient smoothness and the condition r > 4. Blow-up is proven using a concavity-type lemma, showing that solutions blow up in the L∞-norm of |∇w| when the initial energy E(0) is negative and a certain inequality on F'(u) holds. The paper notes that when β is taken as the Dirac measure, the model reduces to the quasilinear wave equation of conventional elasticity. The work extends prior one-dimensional nonlinear nonlocal Boussinesq-type results to two dimensions. The paper is purely theoretical and contains no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational simulations. It is supported by TUBITAK under project TBAG-110R002. The main contributions are the well-posedness theory, the global existence criterion, and the finite-time blow-up result, all grounded in functional analysis and energy methods.
